A transverse pulse on a stretched string travels with \(v = \sqrt{T/\mu}\), where \(\mu\) is the linear mass density.

Linear mass density: \(\mu = \dfrac{2.50\,\text{kg}}{20.0\,\text{m}} = 0.125\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).

Speed: \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{200\,\text{N}}{0.125\,\text{kg m}^{-1}}} = \sqrt{1600} = 40\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Time to cross the string: \(t = \dfrac{L}{v} = \dfrac{20.0\,\text{m}}{40\,\text{m s}^{-1}}\).

The disturbance takes \(t = 0.50\,\text{s}\) to reach the other end.

The total delay is the time the stone takes to fall plus the time the sound takes to climb back.

Fall from rest through \(h = 300\,\text{m}\): \(h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt_{1}^{2}\), so

\(t_{1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 300\,\text{m}}{9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}}} = \sqrt{61.22\,\text{s}^{2}} = 7.82\,\text{s}\).

Sound travels the same \(300\,\text{m}\) upward at \(340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\):

\(t_{2} = \dfrac{300\,\text{m}}{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}} = 0.88\,\text{s}\).

Total time after the stone is dropped: \(t = t_{1} + t_{2} = 7.82 + 0.88\).

The splash is heard about \(8.7\,\text{s}\) after the stone is dropped.

For a transverse wave on a stretched wire, \(v = \sqrt{T/\mu}\), so \(T = \mu v^{2}\).

Linear mass density: \(\mu = \dfrac{2.10\,\text{kg}}{12.0\,\text{m}} = 0.175\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).

Required wave speed: \(v = 343\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

\(T = 0.175\,\text{kg m}^{-1} \times (343\,\text{m s}^{-1})^{2} = 0.175 \times 1.176 \times 10^{5}\,\text{N}\).

The tension required is \(T = 2.06 \times 10^{4}\,\text{N}\).

For one mole of an ideal gas of molar mass \(M\) occupying volume \(V\), \(PV = RT\) and \(\rho = M/V\), so

\(\dfrac{P}{\rho} = \dfrac{PV}{M} = \dfrac{RT}{M}\).

Substituting in \(v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}\) gives

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma RT}{M}}\),

in which the pressure has cancelled out altogether.

At a fixed temperature, compressing the air raises \(P\) but raises \(\rho\) in exactly the same proportion, so the ratio \(P/\rho\) — and hence the speed — is unchanged.

The speed of sound in air is independent of pressure, because \(P\) and \(\rho\) change together at constant temperature and only their ratio enters the formula.

Using \(P/\rho = RT/M\) for an ideal gas, the formula becomes

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma RT}{M}}\).

Here \(\gamma\), \(R\) and \(M\) are fixed for a given gas, so

\(v \propto \sqrt{T}\),

with \(T\) the absolute temperature.

Physically, raising the temperature raises the mean molecular speed, and a sound wave is passed on by molecular collisions, so the disturbance is relayed faster.

The speed of sound in air increases with temperature, in proportion to the square root of the absolute temperature.

At a given pressure and temperature, adding water vapour to air replaces some of the heavier molecules by lighter ones: the molar mass of water is \(18\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\) against about \(29\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\) for dry air.

By Avogadro's law, equal volumes at the same \(P\) and \(T\) contain equal numbers of molecules, so replacing air molecules by lighter water molecules lowers the density:

\(\rho_{\text{moist}} < \rho_{\text{dry}}\).

Since \(P\) and \(\gamma\) are essentially unchanged, and

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}}\),

a smaller density gives a larger speed.

The speed of sound in air increases with humidity, because moist air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature.

No, the converse is not true. Appearing in the combination \(x \pm vt\) is necessary but not sufficient: a physically acceptable wave function must also be single-valued, finite and bounded for every \(x\) at every \(t\), because it represents a real displacement of the medium.

For \(y = (x - vt)^{2}\): the function is single-valued, but it grows without limit as \(|x - vt|\) becomes large, and at a fixed instant it is already infinite as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

An unbounded displacement is physically impossible, so \((x - vt)^{2}\) cannot represent a travelling wave.

No, the converse is not true. The combination \(x \pm vt\) is necessary but not sufficient: the function must in addition be single-valued, finite and bounded everywhere at all times.

For \(y = \log\left[(x + vt)/x_{0}\right]\): the logarithm is not defined at all when \(x + vt < 0\), it diverges to \(-\infty\) as \(x + vt \to 0\), and it grows without limit as \(x + vt \to \infty\).

Since it is neither finite nor defined everywhere, \(\log\left[(x + vt)/x_{0}\right]\) cannot represent a travelling wave.

But \(1/(x+vt)\) diverges at \(x = -vt\), and such a point exists at every instant, so (c) fails the very criterion the key states one sentence earlier. The key's verdict refutes its own test. A charitable reading is that it means finite as \(x \to \pm\infty\), which (c) alone passes; this remains a long-contested item, so the reasoning below is given in full rather than a bare verdict. Parts (a) and (b) agree with the key.] No, the converse is not true. Containing \(x \pm vt\) is necessary but not sufficient: a wave function must also be single-valued, finite and bounded for all \(x\) and all \(t\).

For \(y = 1/(x + vt)\): the function blows up at \(x = -vt\), where the displacement would become infinite.

Because it is not finite everywhere, \(1/(x + vt)\) cannot represent a travelling wave.

The frequency is fixed by the source and is unchanged by reflection or by entering a new medium; only the speed, and hence the wavelength, changes.

\(\nu = 1000\,\text{kHz} = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}\), and \(\lambda = v/\nu\).

(a) The reflected sound travels back through the SAME medium, air, at \(v = 340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\):

\(\lambda_{\text{ref}} = \dfrac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}} = 3.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\).

(b) The transmitted sound travels in water at \(v = 1486\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), with the frequency still \(1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}\):

\(\lambda_{\text{trans}} = \dfrac{1486\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}} = 1.49 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).

(a) \(\lambda_{\text{reflected}} = 3.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\)

(b) \(\lambda_{\text{transmitted}} = 1.49 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\)

Convert to SI: \(v = 1.7\,\text{km s}^{-1} = 1.7 \times 10^{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(\nu = 4.2\,\text{MHz} = 4.2 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}\).

Using \(v = \nu\lambda\),

\(\lambda = \dfrac{v}{\nu} = \dfrac{1.7 \times 10^{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{4.2 \times 10^{6}\,\text{Hz}}\).

The wavelength of the sound in the tissue is \(\lambda = 4.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\) (about \(0.4\,\text{mm}\)).

The given function is \(y = 3.0 \sin (36\,t + 0.018\,x + \pi/4)\) with \(x\), \(y\) in cm and \(t\) in s. Comparing with \(y = a \sin(kx + \omega t + \phi)\): \(a = 3.0\,\text{cm}\), \(k = 0.018\,\text{cm}^{-1}\), \(\omega = 36\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), \(\phi = \pi/4\).

(a) Because \(x\) and \(t\) enter only through the single combination \(0.018x + 36t\), it is a TRAVELLING wave, not a stationary one. A point of constant phase satisfies \(0.018x + 36t = \text{constant}\), so \(x\) must DECREASE as \(t\) increases: the wave travels in the negative \(x\) direction, i.e. from right to left. Its speed is

\(v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{36\,\text{rad s}^{-1}}{0.018\,\text{cm}^{-1}} = 2000\,\text{cm s}^{-1} = 20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

(b) Amplitude \(a = 3.0\,\text{cm} = 0.03\,\text{m}\); frequency \(\nu = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{36}{2\pi} = 5.73\,\text{Hz}\).

(c) The initial phase is the value of the argument at \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\), namely \(\phi = \pi/4\,\text{rad} = 45^{\circ}\).

(d) Successive crests are one wavelength apart:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2\pi}{0.018\,\text{cm}^{-1}} = 349\,\text{cm} = 3.49\,\text{m}\).

(a) Travelling wave, moving in the negative \(x\) direction (right to left) at \(20\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(b) Amplitude \(3.0\,\text{cm} = 0.03\,\text{m}\), frequency \(5.73\,\text{Hz}\)

(c) Initial phase at the origin \(= \pi/4\,\text{rad}\ (45^{\circ})\)

(d) Least distance between successive crests \(= \lambda = 3.49\,\text{m}\)

For the wave \(y = 3.0 \sin (36\,t + 0.018\,x + \pi/4)\), fixing \(x\) leaves a pure sinusoid in \(t\):

\(y(t) = 3.0 \sin\left(36\,t + \delta\right)\,\text{cm}\), where \(\delta = 0.018\,x + \pi/4\).

At \(x = 0\): \(\delta = \pi/4 = 0.785\,\text{rad}\).

At \(x = 2\,\text{cm}\): \(\delta = \pi/4 + 0.036\,\text{rad}\).

At \(x = 4\,\text{cm}\): \(\delta = \pi/4 + 0.072\,\text{rad}\).

So each graph is a sine curve of the same amplitude \(3.0\,\text{cm}\) and the same period

\(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{36} = 0.175\,\text{s}\),

and the three differ only by the small constant phase shifts above — the curves are the same sinusoid slid slightly along the time axis (the shifts are so small, \(0.036\) and \(0.072\,\text{rad}\), that the three plots look almost identical).

All three graphs are sinusoidal, identical in shape. In a travelling wave the oscillations at different points differ only in PHASE; the amplitude and the frequency are the same at every point.

The key contradicts itself inside this one question: it reports (a) as \(6.4\pi\) UNREDUCED, yet its \(\pi/2\) for (d) is only reachable BY reducing \(3\pi/2\) to \(|3\pi/2 - 2\pi| = \pi/2\). Two mechanisms reproduce the printed value exactly — that reduction, or computing \(\lambda/4\) in place of \(3\lambda/4\) — and the evidence does not separate them, so neither is asserted here.] Write the wave as \(y = 2.0 \cos\left(2\pi \times 10\,t - 2\pi \times 0.0080\,x + 2\pi \times 0.35\right)\), with \(x\) in cm.

The propagation constant is \(k = 2\pi \times 0.0080\,\text{cm}^{-1}\), so

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{1}{0.0080}\,\text{cm} = 125\,\text{cm} = 1.25\,\text{m}\).

Two points a distance \(\Delta x\) apart differ in phase by \(\Delta\phi = k\,\Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi\,\Delta x}{\lambda}\).

(b) \(\Delta x = 0.5\,\text{m} = 50\,\text{cm}\): \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi \times \dfrac{50}{125} = 0.8\pi\,\text{rad} = 2.51\,\text{rad}\).

(c) \(\Delta x = \lambda/2\): \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \pi\,\text{rad}\).

(d) \(\Delta x = 3\lambda/4\): \(\Delta\phi = 2\pi \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\,\text{rad}\).

(a) \(6.4\pi\,\text{rad} = 20.1\,\text{rad}\)

(b) \(0.8\pi\,\text{rad} = 2.51\,\text{rad}\)

(c) \(\pi\,\text{rad}\)

(a) In \(y = 0.06 \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}x\right)\cos(120\pi t)\) the position and the time appear in SEPARATE factors, not in the combination \(kx \mp \omega t\). The pattern does not move; only the amplitude \(0.06\sin(2\pi x/3)\) varies from point to point. It is a STATIONARY (standing) wave.

(b) Using \(2\sin A\cos B = \sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)\),

\(y = 0.03\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}x + 120\pi t\right) + \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}x - 120\pi t\right)\right]\),

which is the superposition of two waves of amplitude \(0.03\,\text{m}\) travelling in opposite directions along \(x\). For each of them

\(k = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\,\text{m}^{-1} \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = 3\,\text{m}\),

\(\omega = 120\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1} \Rightarrow \nu = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = 60\,\text{Hz}\),

\(v = \nu\lambda = 60\,\text{Hz} \times 3\,\text{m} = 180\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

(c) Linear mass density: \(\mu = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg}}{1.5\,\text{m}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).

From \(v = \sqrt{T/\mu}\), \(T = \mu v^{2} = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg m}^{-1} \times (180\,\text{m s}^{-1})^{2}\).

(a) A stationary wave

(b) Two waves of amplitude \(0.03\,\text{m}\) moving in opposite directions, each with \(\lambda = 3\,\text{m}\), \(\nu = 60\,\text{Hz}\) and \(v = 180\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(c) \(T = 648\,\text{N}\)

The intended target is Exercise 14.11, whose string is \(1.5\,\text{m}\) long, of which the stated \(0.375\,\text{m}\) is exactly a quarter. A leftover from the edition in which this was Chapter 15.] The string of the previous question carries the standing wave \(y = 0.06 \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}x\right)\cos(120\pi t)\), with \(x\) in m, \(t\) in s and \(L = 1.5\,\text{m}\).

(i)(a) The time dependence is the single common factor \(\cos(120\pi t)\), so every oscillating element repeats after the same period. All points oscillate with the SAME frequency, \(\nu = 120\pi/2\pi = 60\,\text{Hz}\) — except the nodes, which do not oscillate at all.

(i)(b) Because that same factor \(\cos(120\pi t)\) multiplies every element, all points reach their extreme displacements at the same instants. Over \(0 \le x \le 1.5\,\text{m}\) the factor \(\sin(2\pi x/3)\) runs from \(\sin 0\) to \(\sin\pi\) and never changes sign, so every point of this string moves in the SAME phase (points in adjacent loops of a longer string would be exactly out of phase by \(\pi\)).

(i)(c) The amplitude is \(0.06\left|\sin(2\pi x/3)\right|\), which depends on \(x\): it is zero at the clamped ends and largest at the middle. So the points do NOT all have the same amplitude.

(ii) At \(x = 0.375\,\text{m}\),

\(A = 0.06 \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi \times 0.375}{3}\right) = 0.06 \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 0.06 \times 0.707\,\text{m}\).

(i)(a) Yes, all points (other than the nodes) oscillate with the same frequency, \(60\,\text{Hz}\).

(i)(b) Yes, all the oscillating points of this string are in the same phase.

(i)(c) No, the amplitude varies from point to point.

(ii) \(A = 4.24 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\)

A travelling wave must have \(x\) and \(t\) bound together in the combination \(x \mp vt\); a stationary wave has them in separate factors, of the form (function of \(x\)) \(\times\) (function of \(t\)).

In \(y = 2\cos(3x)\sin(10t)\) the position and time appear in separate factors. This is exactly the standing-wave form \(2a\cos kx \sin \omega t\), with \(k = 3\) and \(\omega = 10\): the profile does not move, and the amplitude \(2\cos 3x\) is fixed at each point, vanishing at the nodes.

This represents a STATIONARY wave.

Here \(y = 2\sqrt{x - vt}\) does contain \(x\) and \(t\) in the combination \(x - vt\), so it passes the first test — but that condition alone is not sufficient.

A displacement must be defined, single-valued and finite for every \(x\) at every \(t\). This function is NOT defined at all wherever \(x < vt\) (the square root of a negative number), and it grows without limit as \(x - vt \to \infty\).

Because it fails to represent a finite displacement everywhere, this function represents NONE of the two — it is not a travelling wave and not a stationary wave.

Both terms of \(y = 3\sin(5x - 0.5t) + 4\cos(5x - 0.5t)\) are functions of the single combination \((5x - 0.5t)\).

Writing \(3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = R\sin(\theta + \phi)\) with \(R = \sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = 5\) and \(\tan\phi = 4/3\),

\(y = 5\sin\left(5x - 0.5t + \phi\right)\), \(\phi = \tan^{-1}(4/3) = 0.927\,\text{rad}\).

This is a single harmonic wave of amplitude \(5\) units moving in the \(+x\) direction with speed \(v = \omega/k = 0.5/5 = 0.1\) units.

This represents a TRAVELLING wave.

In \(y = \cos x\sin t + \cos 2x\sin 2t\), each term separately has \(x\) and \(t\) in SEPARATE factors, so each term is itself a standing wave: the first with \(k = 1\), \(\omega = 1\), the second with \(k = 2\), \(\omega = 2\).

The two have different wave numbers and different frequencies, so their sum cannot be collapsed into a single \(f(x \mp vt)\) and it is not one harmonic standing wave either.

This represents a superposition of TWO STATIONARY waves — it is a stationary-wave pattern, not a travelling wave.

First get the length of the wire from its mass and its linear mass density:

\(L = \dfrac{m}{\mu} = \dfrac{3.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg}}{4.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg m}^{-1}} = 0.875\,\text{m}\).

(a) A wire clamped at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode with \(L = \lambda/2\), so \(\lambda = 2L = 1.75\,\text{m}\) and

\(v = \nu\lambda = 45\,\text{Hz} \times 1.75\,\text{m} = 78.75\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

(b) From \(v = \sqrt{T/\mu}\),

\(T = \mu v^{2} = 4.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{kg m}^{-1} \times (78.75\,\text{m s}^{-1})^{2}\).

(a) \(v = 78.8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(b) \(T = 248\,\text{N}\)

The tube is closed by the piston at one end and open at the other, so the air column resonates when its length is an odd number of quarter wavelengths. The question directs that edge effects be neglected, so the first resonance is exactly a quarter wavelength:

\(l_1 = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), so \(\lambda = 4 l_1 = 4 \times 0.255\,\text{m} = 1.02\,\text{m}\).

The frequency is that of the fork and is unchanged by the tube, \(\nu = 340\,\text{Hz}\). Hence

\(v = \nu\lambda = 340\,\text{Hz} \times 1.02\,\text{m} = 347\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

Note that the two observed lengths do not close exactly under this assumption: the next resonance would be the third harmonic at \(3 l_1 = 76.5\,\text{cm}\), against the observed \(79.3\,\text{cm}\). That \(2.8\,\text{cm}\) gap IS the end correction the question tells you to ignore. Eliminating it instead by taking the difference of the two lengths, \(\lambda/2 = 79.3 - 25.5 = 53.8\,\text{cm}\), gives \(v = 366\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) — the better method when edge effects are NOT neglected, but not what this question asks for.

The rod is clamped at its middle, so that point cannot move and is a displacement NODE, while both free ends are displacement ANTINODES.

In the fundamental mode the rod holds just one node with an antinode at each end, so its length is half a wavelength:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2L = 2 \times 1.00\,\text{m} = 2.00\,\text{m}\).

With \(\nu = 2.53\,\text{kHz} = 2.53 \times 10^{3}\,\text{Hz}\),

\(v = \nu\lambda = 2.53 \times 10^{3}\,\text{Hz} \times 2.00\,\text{m}\).

The speed of sound (of longitudinal waves) in steel is \(v = 5.06 \times 10^{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), i.e. about \(5.06\,\text{km s}^{-1}\).

A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only ODD harmonics are possible:

\(\nu_{n} = (2n - 1)\dfrac{v}{4L}\), \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

With \(L = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\) and \(v = 340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\),

\(\dfrac{v}{4L} = \dfrac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{0.80\,\text{m}} = 425\,\text{Hz}\),

so the possible modes are \(425\,\text{Hz}\), \(1275\,\text{Hz}\), \(2125\,\text{Hz}\), and so on. The \(430\,\text{Hz}\) source lies within about \(1\%\) of the first of these, so it is the FUNDAMENTAL (first harmonic) that is resonantly excited. (The data are meant to match exactly: \(v/4L\) equals \(430\,\text{Hz}\) precisely for \(v = 344\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), the speed of sound at about \(22\,^{\circ}\text{C}\).)

If both ends are open, every harmonic of \(v/2L\) is allowed:

\(\nu_{1} = \dfrac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{0.40\,\text{m}} = 850\,\text{Hz}\),

and the higher modes are \(1700\,\text{Hz}\), \(2550\,\text{Hz}\), and so on. Since \(430\,\text{Hz}\) is below even the fundamental of the open pipe, it cannot match any mode.

The \(430\,\text{Hz}\) source excites the FIRST (fundamental) mode of the closed pipe; with both ends open the fundamental rises to \(850\,\text{Hz}\), so the same source will NOT be in resonance with the pipe.
_note: The stem's numbers do not close exactly with the printed speed. With v = 340 m/s the closed-pipe fundamental is 425 Hz, not the 430 Hz of the source; the intended exact match needs v = 344 m/s. The physics answer (first mode; no resonance when both ends are open) is unaffected either way, since 430 Hz is far from 1275 Hz and far below 850 Hz.

A sound wave carries a displacement \(s(x, t)\) of the air elements and, with it, a pressure variation. The excess pressure is set by how much the medium is being compressed, i.e. by the SPATIAL GRADIENT of the displacement:

\(\Delta P = -B\,\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x}\),

where \(B\) is the bulk modulus.

At a displacement NODE the elements do not move, but the elements on the two sides of it move in OPPOSITE directions — alternately towards it and away from it. The layer is therefore alternately squeezed and stretched: \(s = 0\) there, yet \(\left|\partial s/\partial x\right|\) is a maximum, so the pressure variation is largest. That is a pressure ANTINODE.

At a displacement ANTINODE the elements swing with the largest amplitude, but those on either side move together, in the same direction and by nearly the same amount. Nothing is compressed: \(\partial s/\partial x = 0\) there, so the pressure stays at its mean value. That is a pressure NODE.

Since the pressure variation goes as the derivative of the displacement, the two patterns are a quarter wavelength out of step: a displacement node is a pressure antinode, and a displacement antinode is a pressure node.

A bat emits short pulses of ultrasonic sound and listens for the echo reflected back from an obstacle.

The TIME DELAY \(t\) between sending the pulse and receiving the echo fixes the distance, since the sound covers the gap twice: \(d = vt/2\).

The DIRECTION follows from which way the ears face when the echo is loudest, and from the small difference in arrival time and intensity at the two ears.

The SIZE follows from the strength of the returning pulse — a larger obstacle intercepts and returns a larger fraction of the sound — and from how long the echo lasts.

The NATURE of the surface follows from the quality of the echo: how much is absorbed rather than reflected, and how the mixture of frequencies in the returned pulse is altered.

Ultrasonic waves are used because their wavelength is very short, so they are reflected sharply by small objects instead of simply bending around them; this is what lets a bat resolve fine detail and build up a picture of its surroundings without using its eyes.

The PITCH we hear is set by the fundamental frequency, and for the two notes that is the same. But a plucked or bowed string never vibrates in its fundamental alone.

The string is set going in a superposition of many of its normal modes, \(\nu_{n} = n\nu_{1}\), and how strongly each overtone is excited depends on the instrument: on where the string is plucked or bowed, on how it is driven (a bow keeps feeding energy in, a pluck does not), and on the shape, size and material of the body that radiates the sound and favours some harmonics over others.

So the violin note and the sitar note share the same fundamental but carry DIFFERENT relative amplitudes of the higher harmonics. Adding these different mixtures gives waveforms of different shape even though the repetition rate is identical.

The ear responds to that harmonic content, which we perceive as the QUALITY or TIMBRE of the note. It is the difference in the overtones — not in the frequency — that lets us tell the two instruments apart.

The two kinds of wave call on different elastic properties of the medium.

A TRANSVERSE wave displaces the elements sideways, so successive layers are slid over one another. Restoring that shape needs a resistance to SHEAR, i.e. a non-zero shear (rigidity) modulus. Solids have one — their atoms sit in a lattice and a sideways displacement of one plane sets up a restoring force from its neighbours.

A LONGITUDINAL wave displaces the elements along the direction of travel, alternately compressing and rarefying the medium. That needs only a resistance to a change in VOLUME, i.e. a non-zero bulk modulus. Solids, liquids and gases all have one, since all of them resist being compressed.

A gas has no shear modulus at all: its molecules are not bound to fixed neighbours, so one layer can slide past another with no restoring force and a sideways disturbance simply dies away instead of propagating.

Hence solids, having both a shear modulus and a bulk modulus, support both transverse and longitudinal waves, while a gas has only a bulk modulus and can carry longitudinal waves alone.

A pulse is not a single harmonic wave. By Fourier's theorem it is a superposition of many harmonic components of different frequencies, and it keeps its shape only so long as they all stay in the same relative phase.

A DISPERSIVE medium is one in which the wave speed depends on frequency, \(v = v(\nu)\). Each Fourier component of the pulse therefore travels at its own speed, and after travelling a distance the components have slipped out of their original phase relationship with one another.

When they are added again they no longer reconstruct the original profile: the pulse broadens and its shape changes as it advances.

So the shape of a pulse is distorted in a dispersive medium because its different frequency components travel at different speeds. In a non-dispersive medium all components move with the same speed, the phase relations are preserved, and the pulse keeps its shape.
